newsitem.title: USA: Study outlines risks of dropping ethanol tax break.
newsitem.headline: Study outlines risks of dropping ethanol tax break.

text.p: U.S. farm incomes and feed grains prices would decline significantly if an ethanol tax incentive was eliminated, according to a study released Wednesday by the office of Iowa Sen. Tom Harkin.

The study was prepared for Harkin, an Iowa Democrat, by researchers at the Food and Agricultural Policy Research Institute. The study found that eliminating ethanol's partial excise tax exemption would cut current levels of ethanol production and destroy a projected increase in ethanol demand.
Harkin's office released the report Wednesday, touting it as a well-balanced defense against recent efforts by other U.S. lawmakers to scrap the tax break.
U.S. Rep. Bill Archer, chairman of the House Ways and Means Committee and an opponent of the ethanol subsidy, has called it "a wasteful use of tax dollars."
The FAPRI study assumed that the current ethanol tax exemption would be eliminated with the start of the 1997/98 crop marketing year.

Without the tax incentive, corn use for ethanol would fall by more than 544 million bushels a year by the 2005/06 crop year. Corn prices at the farm level would fall 10 cents per bushel the first year and 15 cents by 2005, and prices of other feedgrains would also fall, the study said
"While there will be offsets to the loss in ethanol demand, clearly the overall effect will be to reduce the level of corn consumption," the study said.
In a news release, Harkin challenged Archer and other lawmakers opposed to the ethanol subsidy.
"I doubt he'll change his mind about ethanol, but I just wanted to send a little signal to him and to the big oil interests that they're in for a fight if they go after ethanol," Harkin said.
